label: Chapter 4: A Grand Duchy Is Born, 1815 to 1867

units.text: Picture the scene in Vienna in the winter of 1814 and 1815.
Napoleon had been defeated and exiled.
The diplomats of Europe, kings, princes, and ministers in glittering uniforms, gathered for the Congress of Vienna to redraw the map.
Their main goal was simple: make sure France could never again conquer its neighbors.
And one of the ways to do that was to build a strong state on France's northern border.
So they combined what is now the Netherlands and what is now Belgium into a single United Kingdom of the Netherlands, ruled by William of Orange-Nassau, who became King William the First.
William's family had lost its ancestral German lands, so the great powers looked for ways to compensate him.
One of them was Luxembourg.
The diplomats made it a state in its own right.
They raised it to the rank of grand duchy, which was a way of saying it was more than an ordinary duchy and a proper sovereign state with a seat in the new German Confederation.
William would be both King of the Netherlands and Grand Duke of Luxembourg, a so-called personal union, in which the same man wore two crowns over two countries that were otherwise separate.
And so, in 1815, the Grand Duchy of Luxembourg came into being.
It remains the only grand duchy in the world.
But the new state was smaller than the old duchy.
Prussia, the rising power on the Rhine, demanded land, and Luxembourg lost its entire eastern border region, the territory east of the rivers Moselle, Sûre and Our.
This was about a quarter of its area, and it was the second time in the modern era that the country had been carved up.
As part of the deal, the fortress of Luxembourg became a fortress of the German Confederation, and a Prussian garrison moved in.
The Grand Duke ruled the country.
The Prussians held the rock.
Then came 1830, and the great shock.
In Brussels, riots broke out after an opera performance, and within weeks the southern provinces of the United Kingdom of the Netherlands had risen up in a revolution.
They were Catholic and mostly French-speaking, and they resented rule by a Protestant, Dutch-speaking king.
They declared independence as the new Kingdom of Belgium.
Most of Luxembourg joined them.
Luxembourgers took part in the uprising, sent representatives to the Belgian national congress, and for several years almost the whole country was governed from Brussels.
The only exception was the capital, where the Prussian garrison held the fortress firmly in the name of the German Confederation.
For nearly a decade, the fate of Luxembourg was unresolved.
Belgium claimed all of it. The Dutch king claimed all of it.
The great powers met in London and eventually proposed a compromise.
In 1839, after King William finally accepted defeat, a treaty was signed in London that carved the country in two.
The western part of Luxembourg, the French-speaking part, went to Belgium.
It included the towns of Arlon and Bastogne, a name we will meet again in the Second World War.
This was roughly sixty-five percent of the country's territory, and about half its population, something like one hundred and seventy-five thousand people.
What remained was the eastern, German-speaking part, essentially the Luxembourg of today.
Historians still shake their heads at how it was done.
The line was drawn in London, using maps that were out of date and inaccurate, by diplomats who had never visited the places they were dividing.
To compensate the German Confederation for the loss, part of the Dutch province of Limburg was attached to it.
And the Grand Duchy of Luxembourg, which had been a middling European territory, became a small, landlocked, mostly poor country with about one hundred and seventy thousand inhabitants.
But here is the twist. The treaty of 1839 is often described as the moment Luxembourg's independence began.

Because it fixed the borders. For the first time, there was a clear, internationally recognized line around a state called Luxembourg, which is the same line you can cross on a bridge or a country road today.
It was a tragic loss, but it was also a beginning.
The decades that followed were hard.
Luxembourg was a farming country with little industry, and in the 1840s a potato blight and poor harvests pushed many families into hunger.
In 1842, the Grand Duchy joined the German customs union, the Zollverein, which tied its economy to the German states and opened up markets for its goods.
But it also meant that Luxembourg's economic fate was linked to its neighbor across the Moselle.
Many Luxembourgers simply left.
Between about 1840 and 1890, tens of thousands of them emigrated, many to the United States, where they settled in the Midwest, especially in Wisconsin, Minnesota, Iowa, and the area around Chicago.
For a country of fewer than two hundred thousand people, this was an enormous drain.
Meanwhile, the Grand Duchy was slowly learning to govern itself.
In 1841, William the Second, the king who followed William the First, granted Luxembourg its first constitution, creating an assembly of the estates.
In 1848, the year revolutions shook Europe, a more liberal constitution followed.
The Dutch kings were not very interested in their grand duchy.
William the Third, who ruled from 1849, rarely visited, and day to day the country was run by his brother Prince Henry as his representative.
And a national consciousness was waking up.
Writers and poets began composing in Luxembourgish, the Moselle Franconian dialect that ordinary people spoke at home and that had no official status.
In 1859, the poet Michel Lentz wrote a song that Luxembourgers still sing, called the Feierwon, or the Fire Wagon, about the arrival of the railway.
Its refrain contains a line that became a kind of national motto.
It says, in Luxembourgish, Mir wëlle bleiwe wat mir sinn, which means, We want to remain what we are.
In the same decade, Lentz wrote the words to the song that would become the national anthem, Ons Heemecht, or Our Homeland, officially adopted in 1895.
And in 1872, Michel Rodange published Renert, a long satirical poem in Luxembourgish about a crafty fox, which many people consider the country's national epic.
Now we come to the crisis that nearly started a war.
In 1866, Prussia defeated Austria in a short, decisive war, and the German Confederation, which had existed since 1815, was dissolved.
Suddenly, no one was sure what Luxembourg's status was.
Was it part of Germany? Was it independent?
Who owned the fortress, with its Prussian garrison?
Napoleon the Third of France saw an opportunity.
Prussia had just become dramatically more powerful, and he wanted something in return to keep the balance, and to restore French prestige.
He offered to buy Luxembourg from King William the Third of the Netherlands, who was short of money and had little emotional attachment to the place.
William agreed in principle.
But Otto von Bismarck, the Prussian chancellor, was not going to let France take a strategic fortress on the German frontier.
Bismarck made sure that news of the sale leaked, and German public opinion exploded.
Luxembourg is German soil, politicians and newspapers cried.
For a few weeks in the spring of 1867, Europe stood at the edge of war.
In the end, diplomacy won out.
The great powers met in London in May 1867, and they agreed on a settlement that satisfied everyone and no one.

The second Treaty of London, signed on the eleventh of May, declared that Luxembourg was an independent state, under the sovereignty of the House of Orange-Nassau, and that it would be perpetually neutral, under the collective guarantee of the great powers.
The Prussian garrison would leave.
And the fortress, the Gibraltar of the North, would be dismantled, so that no one could use it as a weapon against their neighbors.
After nine hundred years of being a prize, Luxembourg was to be a country at peace.
The question was whether its great neighbors would respect it.
We will find out in the chapters ahead.
